The arithmetic is the hook. When Bonhams sells its California Jewels auction in Los Angeles on July 28, the marquee lot is a 70-carat diamond necklace — pear, oval and marquise stones — estimated to just $50,000, and offered with no reserve.

Seventy carats of graded diamond for the price of one fine solitaire isn't a market on the diamonds; it's a market on the setting, the certification and the story. That's the logic of a no-reserve estate sale: the room, not the price sheet, sets the number.

The catalogue runs 300+ lots, with pieces by Van Cleef & Arpels, Graff and Boucheron. Link in bio.

Gold enters the most consequential week of its summer wound tight — holding the low $4,000s, capped near $4,100, floored around $3,964.

Three top-tier prints land in five days: the Fed decides July 28–29 (a hold at 3.50–3.75% is expected), second-quarter GDP is tracking near 1.7%, and core PCE — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — is seen near 3.3%. The risk is in the tone, not the number.

For the jewelry counter, the level that matters is the floor, not the peak. As long as $3,964 holds, gold stays the value story a nervous shopper is already buying. Link in bio.

The secondary market recovered in the second quarter — and it recovered unevenly. Morgan Stanley's latest read (WatchCharts data, June 29) puts value retention at 15.4% above retail for Patek Philippe, 9.8% for Rolex and 3.0% for Audemars Piguet.

Every other brand the bank tracks trades below list: Cartier −27.4%, Omega −32.3%, IWC −37.9%. And the models are sharper still — Patek's Aquanaut runs ~90% over retail, the Nautilus 74%, while the dressy Calatrava sits 34% below.

A recovery this concentrated is really a flight to the same handful of names. The badge and the reference beat the movement. Link in bio.
